claim: Arp2/3 complex is activated at cortical sites in Schizosaccharomyces pombe to assemble branched actin networks that drive endocytosis.
source: The actin filament nucleator Arp2/3 complex is activated at cortical sites in Schizosaccharomyces pombe to assemble branched actin networks that drive endocytosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about the system being studied.

claim: Arp2/3 complex activators Wsp1 and Dip1 are required for proper actin assembly at endocytic sites.
source: Arp2/3 complex activators Wsp1 and Dip1 are required for proper actin assembly at endocytic sites, but how they coordinately control Arp2/3-mediated actin assembly is unknown.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Dip1 activates Arp2/3 complex without preexisting actin filaments to nucleate 'seed' filaments.
source: Alone, Dip1 activates Arp2/3 complex without preexisting actin filaments to nucleate 'seed' filaments that activate Wsp1-bound Arp2/3 complex, thereby initiating branched actin network assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of Dip1.

claim: Wsp1 requires preexisting filaments to activate Arp2/3 complex.
source: In contrast, because Wsp1 requires preexisting filaments to activate, it has been assumed to function exclusively in propagating actin networks by stimulating branching from preexisting filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of Wsp1.

claim: Wsp1 is important for both propagation and initiation of endocytic actin networks.
source: Here we show that Wsp1 is important not only for propagation but also for initiation of endocytic actin networks.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Wsp1 synergizes with Dip1 to co-activate Arp2/3 complex.
source: Using single molecule total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy we show that Wsp1 synergizes with Dip1 to co-activate Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Synergistic co-activation by Wsp1 and Dip1 does not require preexisting actin filaments.
source: Synergistic co-activation does not require preexisting actin filaments, explaining how Wsp1 contributes to actin network initiation in cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Arp2/3 complex nucleates actin filament networks important in cell motility, differentiation, endocytosis, meiotic spindle positioning, and DNA repair.
source: Arp2/3 complex is an important cytoskeletal regulator that nucleates actin filament networks important in a broad range of cellular processes, including cell motility, differentiation, endocytosis, meiotic spindle positioning, and DNA repair (Goley and Welch, 2006; Hurst et al., 2019; Rotty et al., 2013; Yi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Multiple classes of nucleation promoting factors (NPFs) activate Arp2/3 complex, including WASP family proteins (Type I NPFs), cortactin and related proteins (Type II NPFs), and WISH/DIP/SPIN90 (WDS) family proteins.
source: Multiple classes of nucleation promoting factors (NPFs), including WASP family proteins (Type I NPFs), cortactin and related proteins (Type II NPFs), and WISH/DIP/SPIN90 (WDS) family proteins, activate the nucleation activity of Arp2/3 complex in response to cellular signals (Goley and Welch, 2006; Wagner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Actin networks assembled by Arp2/3 complex frequently contain multiple classes of NPFs with nonredundant roles in actin assembly.
source: In vitro, activated NPFs can function independently to stimulate actin filament nucleation by Arp2/3 complex, but in cells, actin networks assembled by Arp2/3 complex frequently contain multiple classes of NPFs with nonredundant roles in actin assembly (Galletta et al., 2008; Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011; Sirotkin et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At sites of endocytosis in S. pombe, Arp2/3 complex nucleates the assembly of branched actin networks that drive invagination of the plasma membrane.
source: At sites of endocytosis in Schizosaccharomyces pombe, Arp2/3 complex nucleates the assembly of branched actin networks that drive invagination of the plasma membrane (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The activity of Arp2/3 complex at endocytic sites can be controlled by at least three distinct NPFs: Wsp1, Dip1, and Myo1.
source: The activity of Arp2/3 complex at endocytic sites can be controlled by at least three distinct NPFs: Wsp1, Dip1, and Myo1 (Sirotkin et al., 2005; Wagner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Analysis of mutant or knockout strains of Wsp1 and Dip1 suggests that activation of Arp2/3 complex by both of these NPFs is required for normal endocytic actin assembly.
source: Analysis of mutant or knockout strains of Wsp1 and Dip1 suggests that activation of Arp2/3 complex by both of these NPFs is required for normal endocytic actin assembly (Basu and Chang, 2011; Sirotkin et al., 2005; Wagner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Wsp1 has a characteristic VCA motif at its C-terminus that is sufficient for activation of Arp2/3 complex.
source: Wsp1, the S. pombe member of the WASP family NPFs, has a characteristic VCA motif at its C-terminus that is sufficient for activation of Arp2/3 complex (Higgs and Pollard, 2001; Sirotkin et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The CA segment within the VCA motif binds Arp2/3 complex at two sites.
source: The CA segment within this motif binds Arp2/3 complex at two sites (Boczkowska et al., 2014; Luan et al., 2018b; Padrick et al., 2011; Ti et al., 2011; Zimmet et al., 2020), while the V segment binds actin monomers, which Wsp1 must recruit to the complex to trigger nucleation (Chereau et al., 2005; Marchand et al., 2001; Rohatgi et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The V segment binds actin monomers, which Wsp1 must recruit to the complex to trigger nucleation.
source: The CA segment within this motif binds Arp2/3 complex at two sites (Boczkowska et al., 2014; Luan et al., 2018b; Padrick et al., 2011; Ti et al., 2011; Zimmet et al., 2020), while the V segment binds actin monomers, which Wsp1 must recruit to the complex to trigger nucleation (Chereau et al., 2005; Marchand et al., 2001; Rohatgi et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Wsp1-bound Arp2/3 complex must bind to a preexisting actin filament to stimulate nucleation.
source: Importantly, the Wsp1-bound Arp2/3 complex must also bind to a preexisting actin filament to stimulate nucleation (Achard et al., 2010; Machesky et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2013a; Wagner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The requirement for preexisting filaments ensures that Wsp1 creates branched actin filaments when it activates Arp2/3 complex.
source: This requirement ensures that Wsp1 creates branched actin filaments when it activates Arp2/3 complex, but also means a preformed filament must be provided to seed assembly of the network.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the requirement for preexisting filaments.

claim: Dip1 uses an armadillo repeat domain to bind and activate Arp2/3 complex.
source: Dip1, like the other members of the WISH/DIP/SPIN90 (WDS) family proteins, uses an armadillo repeat domain to bind and activate Arp2/3 complex (Luan et al., 2018a; Shaaban et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dip1 does not require a preexisting actin filament to trigger nucleation.
source: Unlike Wsp1, Dip1 does not require a preexisting actin filament to trigger nucleation (Wagner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Dip1-mediated activation of Arp2/3 complex creates linear filaments instead of branches.
source: Therefore, Dip1-mediated activation of Arp2/3 complex creates linear filaments instead of branches (Wagner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Linear filaments nucleated by Dip1-activated Arp2/3 complex can activate Wsp1-bound Arp2/3 complex.
source: Importantly, the linear filaments nucleated by Dip1-activated Arp2/3 complex can activate Wsp1-bound Arp2/3 complex, which creates new branched actin filaments that activate subsequent rounds of Wsp1-Arp2/3-mediated branching nucleation (Balzer et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In dip1Δ strains, the rate of initiation of new patches is markedly decreased.
source: For instance, in dip1Δ strains, the rate of initiation of new patches is markedly decreased, but once an endocytic actin network is initiated, it assembles rapidly, suggesting Dip1 is important for seeding but not propagation of the network (Basu and Chang, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Once an endocytic actin network is initiated in dip1Δ strains, it assembles rapidly.
source: For instance, in dip1Δ strains, the rate of initiation of new patches is markedly decreased, but once an endocytic actin network is initiated, it assembles rapidly, suggesting Dip1 is important for seeding but not propagation of the network (Basu and Chang, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of the Wsp1 CA segment motif causes failure of endocytic actin patches to internalize.
source: Further, deletion of the Wsp1 CA segment motif causes failure of endocytic actin patches to internalize, a process thought to be dependent on the propagation of branches (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Biochemical and structural data suggested that Dip1 and Wsp1 might simultaneously bind Arp2/3 complex.
source: Specifically, biochemical and structural data suggested that the two NPFs might simultaneously bind Arp2/3 complex, so they may potentially synergize to activate nucleation (Luan et al., 2018a; Luan et al., 2018b; Wagner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In wild-type cells, Fim1-marked actin patches accumulate in cortical puncta over ~5 s before moving inward and simultaneously disassembling.
source: In wild-type cells, Fim1-marked actin patches accumulate in cortical puncta over ~5 s before moving inward and simultaneously disassembling (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—video 1; Berro and Pollard, 2014; Sirotkin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 1 and citations to prior literature.

claim: The Dip1 deletion strain showed a significant reduction in the patch initiation rate compared to the wild-type strain (0.030 versus 0.0076 patches/s/µM2).
source: As expected based on previous results, the Dip1 deletion strain showed a significant reduction in the patch initiation rate compared to the wild-type strain (0.030 versus 0.0076 patches/s/µM2) and a corresponding decrease in the number of actin patches in the cell (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—video 2; Basu and Chang, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 1D and E and a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Dip1 deletion strain showed a corresponding decrease in the number of actin patches in the cell.
source: As expected based on previous results, the Dip1 deletion strain showed a significant reduction in the patch initiation rate compared to the wild-type strain (0.030 versus 0.0076 patches/s/µM2) and a corresponding decrease in the number of actin patches in the cell (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—video 2; Basu and Chang, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 1D and E and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Once actin assembly was initiated in dip1Δ cells, Fim1-GFP accumulated more rapidly than in the wild-type strain.
source: However, once actin assembly was initiated, Fim1-GFP accumulated more rapidly than in the wild-type strain (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The observations in dip1Δ cells are consistent with previously reported measurements.
source: These observations are consistent with previously reported measurements (Basu and Chang, 2011) and suggest that Dip1 contributes to the initiation but not the propagation of branched endocytic actin networks.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Dip1 contributes to the initiation but not the propagation of branched endocytic actin networks.
source: These observations are consistent with previously reported measurements (Basu and Chang, 2011) and suggest that Dip1 contributes to the initiation but not the propagation of branched endocytic actin networks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 1 and prior literature.

claim: While dip1 deletion caused increased Fim1-GFP to accumulate in individual patches, the ratio of the total actin in patches versus total actin in the cell decreased in the dip1Δ strain because fewer patches were initiated.
source: We note that while dip1 deletion caused increased Fim1-GFP to accumulate in individual patches (Figure 1B), the ratio of the total actin in patches versus total actin in the cell decreased in the dip1Δ strain because fewer patches were initiated.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduced rate of actin patch assembly in dip1Δ cells cannot be explained by excess filamentous actin in the patches depleting the concentration of soluble actin monomers in the cytoplasm.
source: Therefore, the reduced rate of actin patch assembly cannot be explained by excess filamentous actin in the patches depleting the concentration of soluble actin monomers in the cytoplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the wsp1ΔCA mutant the average time between the first appearance of Fim1-GFP and when it reaches peak concentration increased from 5.1 to 6.7 s.
source: In the wsp1ΔCA mutant the average time between the first appearance of Fim1-GFP and when it reaches peak concentration, which we refer to here as the Fim1 assembly time, increased from 5.1 to 6.7 s, consistent with another recent study (Figure 1B and C; Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 1B and C and a citation to prior literature.

claim: The wsp1ΔCA mutation decreased the percentage of actin patches that internalized.
source: In addition, the wsp1ΔCA mutation decreased the percentage of actin patches that internalized (Figure 1F, Figure 1—video 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: The observations in wsp1ΔCA cells are consistent with a role for Wsp1 in the propagation of branched actin during endocytosis.
source: These observations are consistent with a role for Wsp1 in the propagation of branched actin during endocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 1.

claim: wsp1ΔCA cells showed a 40% decrease in the rate of initiation of new actin patches compared to wild-type cells.
source: However, to our surprise, we found that wsp1ΔCA cells also showed a 40% decrease in the rate of initiation of new actin patches compared to wild-type cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: The defect in patch initiation rate in wsp1ΔCA cells is less than observed in dip1Δ cells.
source: While this defect is less than observed in dip1Δ cells, it suggests – contrary to our initial prediction – that Wsp1 may play a role in initiating new endocytic actin patches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 1D.

claim: Combining wsp1∆CA and dip1∆ in the same strain (dip1∆ wsp1∆CA) did not decrease the actin patch initiation rate more than dip1∆ alone.
source: Combining wsp1∆CA and dip1∆ in the same strain (dip1∆ wsp1∆CA) did not decrease the actin patch initiation rate more than dip1∆ alone (Figure 1D, Figure 1—video 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Wsp1 may contribute to the Dip1-mediated actin patch initiation pathway rather than acting in a separate parallel pathway for initiation of actin assembly.
source: This suggests that Wsp1 may contribute to the Dip1-mediated actin patch initiation pathway rather than acting in a separate parallel pathway for initiation of actin assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 1D.

claim: Previous data showed Dip1 is a more potent activator of Arp2/3 complex than Wsp1.
source: Previous data showed Dip1 is a more potent activator of Arp2/3 complex than Wsp1, and that mixing both Wsp1 and Dip1 in a bulk actin polymerization assay increased the actin polymerization rate, but the reason for the increase was unknown (Wagner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mixing both Wsp1 and Dip1 in a bulk actin polymerization assay increased the actin polymerization rate.
source: Previous data showed Dip1 is a more potent activator of Arp2/3 complex than Wsp1, and that mixing both Wsp1 and Dip1 in a bulk actin polymerization assay increased the actin polymerization rate, but the reason for the increase was unknown (Wagner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: At saturating Dip1 concentration (~30 μM), the addition of Wsp1-VCA increased the maximum polymerization rate in the pyrene actin assembly assays ~1.6-fold over reactions with Dip1 alone.
source: Dip1 approaches saturation above ~30 μM, and at this concentration the addition of Wsp1-VCA increased the maximum polymerization rate in the pyrene actin assembly assays ~1.6-fold over reactions with Dip1 alone (Figure 2A and B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The increased actin polymerization rates in the presence of both NPFs cannot be explained by an additive effect in activating Arp2/3 complex, but instead the NPFs are synergistic.
source: These results suggest that the increased actin polymerization rates in the presence of both NPFs cannot be explained by an additive effect in activating Arp2/3 complex, but instead the NPFs are synergistic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Synergistic activation of Arp2/3 complex by Dip1 and Wsp1 results in the nucleation of linear rather than branched actin filaments.
source: These data demonstrate that synergistic activation of Arp2/3 complex by the two NPFs results in the nucleation of linear rather than branched actin filaments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Synergistic co-activation by both NPFs does not require a preexisting actin filament.
source: Therefore, we conclude that like Dip1-mediated activation (Wagner et al., 2013), synergistic co-activation by both NPFs does not require a preexisting actin filament.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 2C and D and prior literature.

claim: Under initial reaction conditions (100 nM Arp2/3 complex and 1 μM GST-VCA), synergistic co-activation of the complex by Dip1 and GST-VCA was not detected.
source: Under our initial reaction conditions (100 nM Arp2/3 complex and 1 μM GST-VCA), we did not detect synergistic co-activation of the complex by Dip1 and GST-VCA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: In reactions in which the concentration of Arp2/3 complex was increased 2.5-fold, the number and percentage of pointed ends with bound Dip1 increased significantly in the presence of GST-VCA, indicating dimeric (GST) Wsp1-VCA synergizes with Dip1.
source: However, in reactions in which the concentration of Arp2/3 complex was increased 2.5-fold, the number and percentage of pointed ends with bound Dip1 increased significantly in the presence of GST-VCA, indicating dimeric (GST) Wsp1-VCA synergizes with Dip1 (Figure 2E and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Both dimeric and monomeric Wsp1-VCA significantly decrease the concentration of Dip1 required to saturate the reaction.
source: These data showed that both dimeric and monomeric Wsp1-VCA significantly decrease the concentration of Dip1 required to saturate the reaction (Figure 2H, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2H.

claim: Unlike monomeric Wsp1-VCA, dimeric Wsp1-VCA did not increase the maximum polymerization rate at saturating Dip1.
source: However, unlike monomeric Wsp1-VCA, dimeric Wsp1-VCA did not increase the maximum polymerization rate at saturating Dip1.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2H.

claim: Monomeric Wsp1 is more potent in its synergy with Dip1 than dimeric Wsp1.
source: These data demonstrate that monomeric Wsp1 is more potent in its synergy with Dip1 than dimeric Wsp1, and point to differences in the mechanism of synergistic activation between monomeric and dimeric Wsp1-VCA (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 2H.

claim: The simple model (model i) produced simulated time polymerization courses that fit the data poorly compared to the measured time courses.
source: This simple model produced simulated time polymerization courses that fit the data poorly compared to the measured time courses (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: Models with one or more actin monomer-binding steps before creation of the nucleus produced simulated polymerization time courses that fit the data significantly better than the reaction pathway without actin monomer collisions.
source: These models produced simulated polymerization time courses that fit the data significantly better than the reaction pathway without actin monomer collisions (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 3C and D and supplementary figures.

claim: The pathway with one actin monomer-binding step fits the data most closely.
source: The pathway with one actin monomer-binding step fits the data most closely, but the fits with two or three monomer-binding steps also improved the fit over the reaction pathway without actin monomer binding (Figure 3D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: Actin monomer binding to the Dip1-bound Arp2/3 complex stimulates activation.
source: These data suggest that actin monomer binding to the Dip1-bound Arp2/3 complex stimulates activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 3.

claim: While adding Wsp1-VCA to actin polymerization reactions containing saturating Dip1 increased the maximal polymerization rate ~1.6-fold compared to reactions without Wsp1, addition of Wsp1-CA had little or no effect on the maximum polymerization rate.
source: We found that while adding Wsp1-VCA to actin polymerization reactions containing saturating Dip1 increased the maximal polymerization rate ~1.6-fold compared to reactions without Wsp1, addition of Wsp1-CA had little or no effect on the maximum polymerization rate (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Actin monomer recruitment by Wsp1 is required for potent synergy with Dip1.
source: Therefore, we conclude that actin monomer recruitment by Wsp1 is required for potent synergy with Dip1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Wsp1-CA slightly decreased the concentration of Dip1 required for half maximal saturation (K1/2), suggesting that it influences one or more of the activation steps.
source: Wsp1-CA slightly decreased the concentration of Dip1 required for half maximal saturation (K1/2), suggesting that it influences one or more of the activation steps (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The influence of Wsp1-CA on K1/2 was small compared to the reduction in the K1/2 of Dip1 caused by Wsp1 with a V region.
source: However, this influence was small compared to the reduction in the K1/2 of Dip1 caused by Wsp1 with a V region (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Simulations that only floated the off rate (k−10) for the actin monomer bound to the Dip1-Arp2/3 assembly fit the data poorly, indicating the synergy between Wsp1 and Dip1 cannot be explained by increased affinity of actin monomers for the Dip1-Arp2/3 assembly alone.
source: These simulations fit the data poorly, indicating the synergy between Wsp1 and Dip1 cannot be explained by increased affinity of actin monomers for the Dip1-Arp2/3 assembly alone (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4B and C.

claim: When the dissociation constant for actin monomers (k−10) and either the koff of Dip1 for Arp2/3 complex (k−9) or the rate constant for the activation step (k11) (or all three) were floated, the simulations closely matched the measured polymerization time courses.
source: However, when we floated the dissociation constant for actin monomers (k−10) and either the koff of Dip1 for Arp2/3 complex (k−9) or the rate constant for the activation step (k11) (or all three), the simulations closely matched the measured polymerization time courses (Figure 4C–E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4C-E and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Multiple steps in the Dip1-mediated activation pathway are accelerated when Wsp1-bound actin monomers are recruited to Arp2/3 complex.
source: These observations suggest that multiple steps in the Dip1-mediated activation pathway are accelerated when Wsp1-bound actin monomers are recruited to Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 4.

claim: Wsp1 and Dip1 alone each stimulate short pitch crosslinking.
source: As expected, Wsp1 and Dip1 alone each stimulate short pitch crosslinking (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Addition of a saturating concentration of Dip1 to a saturating concentration of Wsp1 increased short pitch crosslinking over that observed for either NPF alone.
source: Addition of a saturating concentration of Dip1 to a saturating concentration of Wsp1 increased short pitch crosslinking over that observed for either NPF alone, suggesting the two NPFs together may accelerate this activating step during synergistic activation.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dip1 also increased short pitch crosslinking when added to a reaction containing Wsp1 and actin monomers.
source: Dip1 also increased short pitch crosslinking when added to a reaction containing Wsp1 and actin monomers.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: GST-tagged Wsp1-VCA was able to pull down a significant amount of Dip1 in the presence but not the absence of Arp2/3 complex, indicating formation of a Wsp1-Arp2/3-Dip1 assembly.
source: GST-tagged Wsp1-VCA was able to pull down a significant amount of Dip1 in the presence but not the absence of Arp2/3 complex, indicating formation of a Wsp1-Arp2/3-Dip1 assembly (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Detection of the Dip1-Arp2/3-Wsp1 assembly with the pulldown method required using a mutant Arp2/3 complex that binds with increased affinity to Wsp1, presumably because the Dip1-Arp2/3 interaction is weak.
source: Detection of the Dip1-Arp2/3-Wsp1 assembly with this method required using a mutant Arp2/3 complex that binds with increased affinity to Wsp1, presumably because the Dip1-Arp2/3 interaction is weak (Wagner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Previous measurements of the dynamics of fluorescently labeled NPFs show that Dip1 and Wsp1 colocalize at endocytic sites and arrive with nearly identical timing, ~2 s before actin filaments begin to polymerize.
source: Previous measurements of the dynamics of fluorescently labeled NPFs support this model, because they show that the two NPFs colocalize at endocytic sites and arrive with nearly identical timing, ~2 s before actin filaments begin to polymerize (Basu and Chang, 2011; Sirotkin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The accumulation kinetics of Dip1 are nearly identical to Wsp1; both accumulate over ~6 s as actin assembles, reach a peak concentration just before (~2 s) the actin filament concentration peaks, and then dissociate as the patch begins to internalize and actin disassembles.
source: However, the accumulation kinetics of Dip1 are nearly identical to Wsp1; both accumulate over ~6 s as actin assembles, reach a peak concentration just before (~2 s) the actin filament concentration peaks, and then dissociate as the patch begins to internalize and actin disassembles (Basu and Chang, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The gradual accumulation of Dip1 suggests that it might co-activate Arp2/3 complex with Wsp1 well after actin polymerization has been initiated and throughout the assembly/propagation of the actin patch.
source: The gradual accumulation of Dip1 suggests that it might co-activate Arp2/3 complex with Wsp1 well after actin polymerization has been initiated and throughout the assembly/propagation of the actin patch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the accumulation kinetics of Dip1.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, both inhibitors and activators of the WASP family protein Las17 have been identified.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, both inhibitors and activators of the WASP family protein Las17 have been identified (Goode et al., 2015), and recent experiments suggest that clustering Las17 at high concentrations at endocytic sites might trigger its activity (Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent experiments suggest that clustering Las17 at high concentrations at endocytic sites might trigger its activity.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, both inhibitors and activators of the WASP family protein Las17 have been identified (Goode et al., 2015), and recent experiments suggest that clustering Las17 at high concentrations at endocytic sites might trigger its activity (Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Building evidence suggests that homologues of the proteins that regulate Las17 in S. cerevisiae may control Wsp1 activity in S. pombe.
source: Building evidence suggests that homologues of the proteins that regulate Las17 in S. cerevisiae may control Wsp1 activity in S. pombe (Arasada and Pollard, 2011; MacQuarrie et al., 2019), perhaps at least partially by clustering it at endocytic sites.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activators that turn on Wsp1 could also indirectly stimulate Dip1.
source: Almost nothing is known about the regulation of Dip1, but we show here that Wsp1 synergizes with Dip1, so activators that turn on Wsp1 could also indirectly stimulate Dip1 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the synergy between Wsp1 and Dip1.

claim: The N-terminal ~160 amino acids of Dip1 is not required for activity.
source: For instance, the N-terminal ~160 amino acids of Dip1 is not required for activity (Wagner et al., 2013), but this segment is relatively well conserved among yeast, so it may play a role in localizing or regulating Dip1 independent of Wsp1.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The N-terminal ~160 amino acids of Dip1 is relatively well conserved among yeast, so it may play a role in localizing or regulating Dip1 independent of Wsp1.
source: For instance, the N-terminal ~160 amino acids of Dip1 is not required for activity (Wagner et al., 2013), but this segment is relatively well conserved among yeast, so it may play a role in localizing or regulating Dip1 independent of Wsp1.
evidence: This is speculation based on sequence conservation.

claim: Electron microscopy studies indicate that endocytic actin networks are branched.
source: Electron microscopy studies indicate that endocytic actin networks are branched (Young et al., 2004), and the highly dendritic nature of these filamentous networks is thought to allow them to drive invagination of the plasma membrane (Lacy et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The highly dendritic nature of endocytic actin networks is thought to allow them to drive invagination of the plasma membrane.
source: Electron microscopy studies indicate that endocytic actin networks are branched (Young et al., 2004), and the highly dendritic nature of these filamentous networks is thought to allow them to drive invagination of the plasma membrane (Lacy et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Wsp1 creates a branched actin filament when it activates Arp2/3 complex on its own.
source: Wsp1 creates a branched actin filament when it activates Arp2/3 complex on its own, but we show here that when Wsp1 activates the complex with Dip1 it creates a linear actin filament.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Wsp1.

claim: When Wsp1 activates Arp2/3 complex with Dip1 it creates a linear actin filament.
source: Wsp1 creates a branched actin filament when it activates Arp2/3 complex on its own, but we show here that when Wsp1 activates the complex with Dip1 it creates a linear actin filament.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Cells may need to limit synergistic activation of Arp2/3 complex by Dip1 and Wsp1 to preserve the dendritic nature of endocytic actin networks.
source: This observation suggests that cells may need to limit synergistic activation of Arp2/3 complex by Dip1 and Wsp1 to preserve the dendritic nature of endocytic actin networks.
evidence: This is speculation based on the finding that synergistic activation produces linear filaments.

claim: When Dip1 activates on its own, it remains bound to Arp2/3 complex long after nucleation, unlike Wsp1, so each Dip1 molecule likely only activates one Arp2/3 complex.
source: For instance, we showed previously that when Dip1 activates on its own, it remains bound to Arp2/3 complex long after nucleation, unlike Wsp1, so each Dip1 molecule likely only activates one Arp2/3 complex (Balzer et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Even when it activates with Wsp1, Dip1 stays bound to Arp2/3 complex on the ends of filaments long after nucleation, so Dip1 likely functions as a single turnover NPF in the context of synergistic activation.
source: We found here that even when it activates with Wsp1, Dip1 stays bound to Arp2/3 complex on the ends of filaments long after nucleation, so Dip1 likely functions as a single turnover NPF in the context of synergistic activation (Figure 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The single turnover mechanism of Dip1 may help limit the number of linear filaments created at endocytic sites.
source: Combined with the low concentration of Dip1 at endocytic actin patches, this single turnover mechanism may help limit the number of linear filaments created at endocytic sites (Balzer et al., 2019; Basu and Chang, 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on the single turnover mechanism and low concentration of Dip1.

claim: Actin filaments compete with WDS proteins for binding to Arp2/3 complex.
source: We showed previously that actin filaments compete with WDS proteins for binding to Arp2/3 complex (Luan et al., 2018a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Even if both NPFs are present, activation by Wsp1 alone may dominate once actin filaments begin to accumulate at endocytic sites.
source: Therefore, even if both NPFs are present, activation by Wsp1 alone may dominate once actin filaments begin to accumulate at endocytic sites.
evidence: This is speculation based on competition between actin filaments and WDS proteins.

claim: When Dip1 activates Arp2/3 complex on its own, actin monomers collide with and bind to the Dip1-Arp2/3 complex assembly to help create the nucleation-competent state.
source: Our simulations of actin polymerization kinetics indicate that when Dip1 activates Arp2/3 complex on its own, actin monomers collide with and bind to the Dip1-Arp2/3 complex assembly to help create the nucleation-competent state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic modeling in Figure 3.

claim: Actin monomer binding may help stimulate the short pitch conformational change in the Dip1-Arp2/3 complex assembly.
source: While the function of bound actin monomers is uncertain, our crosslinking data indicate that actin monomer binding may help stimulate the short pitch conformational change in the Dip1-Arp2/3 complex assembly.
evidence: This is speculation based on the crosslinking data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cryo EM structure of activated Arp2/3 complex with Dip1 bound reveals an intra-subunit conformational change called flattening.
source: The cryo EM structure of activated Arp2/3 complex with Dip1 bound also reveals an intra-subunit conformational change that might be stimulated by binding of actin monomers to the Dip1-Arp2/3 complex assembly (Shaaban et al., 2020). This structural change, called flattening, brings Arp2 and Arp3 closer to the conformation that actin subunits adopt in filaments, allowing them to mimic an actin dimer.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A recent study on the human WDS protein, SPIN90, shows that interaction of SPIN90 with the formin mDia1 increases the ability of SPIN90 to trigger nucleation by Arp2/3 complex.
source: Importantly, we note that a recent study on the human WDS protein, SPIN90, shows that interaction of SPIN90 with the formin mDia1 increases the ability of SPIN90 to trigger nucleation by Arp2/3 complex (Cao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Synergy between mDia1 and SPIN90 may occur because mDia1 can recruit actin monomers to the nascent nucleus, using a mechanism analogous to the mechanism of synergy between Dip1 and Wsp1.
source: Synergy between mDia1 and SPIN90 may occur because mDia1 can recruit actin monomers to the nascent nucleus, using a mechanism analogous to the mechanism of synergy between Dip1 and Wsp1 we propose here (Cao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation based on the similarity to the Dip1-Wsp1 mechanism.

claim: Direct tethering of actin monomers by monomeric Wsp1 potently accelerates activation of Arp2/3 complex by Dip1, allowing the two NPFs to synergize.
source: We show here that direct tethering of actin monomers by monomeric Wsp1 potently accelerates activation of Arp2/3 complex by Dip1, allowing the two NPFs to synergize.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 2-4.

claim: A kinetic model that accounted for the increased effective concentration (by decreasing the off rate of actin monomers for the Dip1-Arp2/3 assembly) could not fully explain the acceleration of actin polymerization in reactions containing both NPFs.
source: However, a kinetic model that accounted for the increased effective concentration (by decreasing the off rate of actin monomers for the Dip1-Arp2/3 assembly) could not fully explain the acceleration of actin polymerization in reactions containing both NPFs (Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: To accurately simulate synergistic activation, models allowed Wsp1-recruited actin to either increase the affinity of Dip1 for Arp2/3 complex or accelerate the final activation step.
source: To accurately simulate synergistic activation, our models allowed Wsp1-recruited actin to either increase the affinity of Dip1 for Arp2/3 complex or accelerate the final activation step (Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Crosslinking data suggest that Wsp1-recruited actin monomers may stimulate the activating step (k11 in the simulations) more rapidly than randomly colliding and binding actin monomers.
source: While it is unclear whether one or both of these additional steps are influenced during synergistic activation, our crosslinking data suggest that Wsp1-recruted actin monomers may stimulate the activating step (k11 in our simulations) more rapidly than randomly colliding and binding actin monomers.
evidence: This is speculation based on the crosslinking data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Wsp1 dimerized by GST showed significantly less synergy with Dip1 than monomeric Wsp1.
source: A surprising result of this work is that Wsp1 dimerized by GST showed significantly less synergy with Dip1 than monomeric Wsp1.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: While dimerized Wsp1 moderately decreased the amount of Dip1 required to reach half maximal saturation (K1/2), at saturating Dip1, the maximum polymerization rate was less with GST-Wsp1-VCA than without it.
source: While dimerized Wsp1 moderately decreased the amount of Dip1 required to reach half maximal saturation (K1/2, see Supplementary file 1), at saturating Dip1, the maximum polymerization rate was less with GST-Wsp1-VCA than without it.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Dimeric WASP proteins can recruit two actin monomers and typically bind ~100–150-fold more tightly to the complex than monomeric WASP proteins.
source: Given that dimeric WASP proteins can recruit two actin monomers and typically bind ~100–150-fold more tightly to the complex than monomeric WASP proteins (Padrick et al., 2011; Padrick et al., 2008), we initially expected that dimeric Wsp1 would have greater synergy with Dip1 than Wsp1 monomers.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Previous biochemical and structural data indicate that WASP proteins – when activating on their own – must be released from nascent branch junctions before nucleation.
source: However, previous biochemical and structural data indicate that WASP proteins – when activating on their own – must be released from nascent branch junctions before nucleation (Helgeson and Nolen, 2013; Smith et al., 2013b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dimeric WASP proteins are thought to release more slowly from branch junctions, thereby decreasing how fast nucleation occurs once WASP is bound compared to monomeric WASP.
source: Because they likely bind the branch junction more tightly (Helgeson and Nolen, 2013), dimeric WASP proteins are thought to release more slowly, thereby decreasing how fast nucleation occurs once WASP is bound compared to monomeric WASP.
evidence: This is speculation based on the tighter binding of dimeric WASP proteins.

claim: Tight binding by dimeric Wsp1 to the nascent linear filament nucleus could slow its release, thereby decreasing the nucleation rate and diminishing synergy between Dip1 and Wsp1.
source: Likewise, tight binding by dimeric Wsp1 to the nascent linear filament nucleus could slow its release, thereby decreasing the nucleation rate and diminishing synergy between Dip1 and Wsp1.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mechanism of WASP protein release.

claim: Recent experiments in budding yeast showed that Las17 is recruited to endocytic sites through a set of multivalent interactions similar to the types of interactions that incorporate WASP proteins into phase separated droplets in vitro.
source: Recent experiments in budding yeast showed that Las17 is recruited to endocytic sites through a set of multivalent interactions similar to the types of interactions that incorporate WASP proteins into phase separated droplets in vitro (Banjade and Rosen, 2014; Li et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It will be important to understand if Wsp1 engages Arp2/3 complex as a monomer or oligomer, as this will significantly influence the kinetics of its activation of the complex alone or with Dip1.
source: Whether or not Wsp1 accumulates in similar phase separated droplets, it will be important to understand if Wsp1 engages Arp2/3 complex as a monomer or oligomer, as this will significantly influence the kinetics of its activation of the complex alone or with Dip1.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.
